intro: Mahler sets aside the Fifth Symphony’s winds and brass for this song without a singer. Strings lean into a melody in F major while harp notes spread beneath them; the quiet ending leads straight into the finale.

sections.label: A · Harp and the violin song
sections.mNote: Long F-major phrases over plucked harp notes

sections.label: B · The strings move more freely
sections.mNote: A warmer G-string melody and a turn towards G♭ major

sections.label: A′ · The harp brings back the song
sections.mNote: The strings slow as the opening tune returns

sections.label: A″ · The violins climb and broaden
sections.mNote: High violin notes above rising cellos and harp

sections.label: Coda · Strings settle into F major
sections.mNote: The harp falls silent before the final chord

relations.label: The opening song returns
relations.basis: The Adagietto’s A–B–A′ outline restores the F-major opening after the contrasting middle span. The later excerpt lies just after the return marked near 415 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.933, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 413 s (cache/form/mahler-5-adagietto.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A melody gathers its breath
cues.text: The violas hold a chord while the harp begins to move. Cellos enter, then the first violins find their long F-major melody. Mahler writes seelenvoll, soulful: the notes lean against the harmony before settling into place.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, Peters full score, plate 9015, p. 178, opening bars: divided violas, harp pickup, cello entry and violin melody marked seelenvoll. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/04/IMSLP13083-Mahler-Symphony_No.5_IV.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mengelberg’s note about Alma
cues.text: Willem Mengelberg writes in his score that the Adagietto is Mahler’s declaration of love to Alma. He says both Mahlers tell him so. In his account, Mahler sends her the manuscript without a covering letter, and she understands.
cues.evidence: Mengelberg’s score annotation (“Statt eines Briefes sandte er ihr dieses im Manuskript: weiter kein Wort dazu. Sie hat es verstanden … Beide haben mir dies erzählt. WM”), quoted at https://www.alma-mahler.com/archiv_semmering_deutsch/presscorner/alma_und_musik.html and, in part, by K. Dawn Grapes: https://fcsymphony.org/mahler-adagietto/ . This is Mengelberg’s account of the manuscript’s meaning; the annotation’s date is not supplied there.

cues.title: Warmth on the G string
cues.text: The middle moves more freely. The first violins play on the G string, with warmth and a full tone, while the harp falls silent. The string melody presses towards G♭ major; a brief return of harp arpeggios helps it swell along the way.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 180, Fliessender at rehearsal 2 (bar 38): violin G-Saite, mit Wärme, grosser Ton; brief harp return in bars 44–46, immediately before the G♭-major key signature at bar 47.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The harp finds its way back
cues.text: The strings slow and die away. Harp triplets return under held chords, and the opening melody begins again at Tempo I. The harp’s small, separate notes make the long string phrases feel suspended in the air.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 181, rehearsal 3 and Tempo I (Molto Adagio): morendo strings, returning harp triplets and the opening melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A funeral and a film
cues.text: In June 1968 Leonard Bernstein conducts the Adagietto at Robert Kennedy’s funeral in New York. Three years later Luchino Visconti makes it the musical centre of Death in Venice. A movement associated with love enters public life as music of farewell.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s performance at St Patrick’s Cathedral, 8 June 1968, and Visconti’s 1971 film: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/

cues.title: The high phrase opens out
cues.text: The violins climb and hold their high notes while the cellos rise beneath them. Mahler asks for broad bow strokes and a full sound. At the crest, the phrase slows further and begins its long descent.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 182: breiter Strich, viel Bogen wechseln, viel Ton and Sehr zurückhaltend around the final climax.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: F major, then straight on
cues.text: The harp has stopped, leaving the strings to ease down into F major. Mahler holds the last chord for a long time, then asks for the Rondo-Finale to follow without a break. This stillness belongs inside a symphony that is about to wake up.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, final bars: harp rests after the last fortissimo chord, strings descend to F major, fermatas marked lang and attacca Rondo-Finale.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The harp leaves the strings alone
transitions.from: A · Harp and the violin song
transitions.to: B · The strings move more freely
transitions.how: The opening phrases settle and the harp stops. At Fliessender, the first violins begin a warmer, more mobile line on the G string. The harmony travels towards G♭ major, with a brief harp return before the new key settles.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, plate 9015, p. 180: rehearsal 2, violin G-Saite instruction and harp return in bars 44–46.

transitions.title: Harp triplets restore the opening song
transitions.from: B · The strings move more freely
transitions.to: A′ · The harp brings back the song
transitions.how: The middle’s string figures slow through zurückhaltend and morendo. The harp re-enters in triplets under sustained string chords. At Tempo I (Molto Adagio) the opening melody returns, with plucked bass notes underneath.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 181, end of the middle section, rehearsal 3 and Tempo I.

transitions.title: Broad bows carry the high notes
transitions.from: A′ · The harp brings back the song
transitions.to: A″ · The violins climb and broaden
transitions.how: Over harp arpeggios, the cello line climbs into the violins’ high phrase. Mahler asks for broad bow strokes as the strings crescendo. The basses change from plucking to bowing, strengthening the harmony beneath the final expansive statement.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, Noch langsamer onwards: rising cellos, breiter Strich, crescendo and arco basses before the final climax.

transitions.title: The strings finish without the harp
transitions.from: A″ · The violins climb and broaden
transitions.to: Coda · Strings settle into F major
transitions.how: The harp strikes its last broad chord and falls silent. Under Sehr zurückhaltend, the strings descend and diminish through the closing harmony into F major. The final fermata is marked long, with attacca Rondo-Finale beneath the basses.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, final system: harp rests, string diminuendo, long fermatas and attacca instruction.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, IV. Adagietto, full score (Peters, plate 9015)
source.locator: Peters score, pp. 178–182: strings and harp; the harp rests through most of the middle, returning briefly in bars 44–46.

timeline.note: Harp arpeggios unfold beneath sustained divided violas; cellos enter before the violin melody.
First violins sing above harp arpeggios, divided inner strings and pizzicato basses.
First violins rest while violas and cellos continue the phrase beneath the harp.
The high melody returns; second violins and violas sustain the inner harmony.
Both violin sections broaden the rising phrase as harp arpeggios spread across registers.
Second violins carry the line while first violins withdraw; harp and lower strings continue.
The more flowing middle begins with strings alone; first violins play warmly on the G string.
Harp briefly rejoins the middle-section swell with widely spaced rising figures.
The harp falls silent again; divided strings sustain the moving middle section.
Harp arpeggios restore the opening texture beneath the returning violin phrase.
High violins and rising cellos stretch the phrase above divided inner strings and harp.
The harp falls silent; strings descend and taper into the final F-major chord.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
